bodies.linkedin:
In the late sixteenth-century, numbers still carried the pejorative connotations associated with necromancy.

Double-entry bookkeeping helped confer cultural authority on numbers by means of the balance. For late sixteenth-century readers, the balance conjured up both the scales of justice and the symmetry of God's world.

This methodical system requires every financial transaction to be recorded with equal and opposite debits and credits. By convention, debits are posted on the left-hand side of a ledger account, and credits are posted on the right-hand side.

Luca Pacioli is often called the father of accounting because he was the first to publish a detailed description of the double-entry system in his 1494 mathematics textbook, Summa de arithmetica, geometria, proportioni et proportionalità.

Accounting systems have evolved from the Farolfi firm's ledger of 1299–1300 to modern requirements for public companies.
bodies.thread:
In the late sixteenth-century, numbers still carried the pejorative connotations associated with necromancy.

Double-entry bookkeeping helped confer cultural authority on numbers by means of the balance.

For late sixteenth-century readers, the balance conjured up both the scales of justice and the symmetry of God's world.

The earliest extant European accounting records following the modern double-entry system come from Amatino Manucci, a Florentine merchant at the end of the 13th century.

The Farolfi firm's ledger of 1299–1300 provides evidence of full double-entry bookkeeping.

Luca Pacioli first codified the double-entry system in his 1494 mathematics textbook, Summa de arithmetica, geometria, proportioni et proportionalità.

Double-entry bookkeeping is a methodical system of recording financial transactions that ensures accuracy and balance through the use of equal and opposite debits and credits.
